brief_context: Home territory of women visiting the E.A.W. Headquarters
brief_extract:
This, of course, is always presented in the way which is most easily grasped by a particular audience. For instance, electricity in the home would make one appeal to teenage girls from a finishing school and a different appeal to women taking a cultural course at the Tropical Community Development Centre of the Y.M.C.A., as they came from such widely separated territories as Sierra Leone, Kenya, Tanganyika, Nigeria, Uganda, Ghana and the Solomon Islands. Modern Systems and Primitive Methods

The English girls engaged in a practical course of meter reading, fuse mending and the re-wiring of plugs, as many of them would expect to tackle these jobs, while the overseas visitors were given a simple explanation of the many ways in which electrical equipment gives women complete emancipation from drudgery in the modern home.

our traditional Christmas dish.

brief_context: Country that presented a report on the congress theme.
brief_extract:
Statements that would be naive in a country with a long history of formal education represent necessary stages of development in a land where such a system is only just beginning, and where large sections of public opinion and ancillary services may still be based on tribal law and custom. Reports were presented on the Congress theme by Canada, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Israel, Netherlands, New Zealand, Norway, Sweden, United Kingdom and the United States of America. Great similarity appeared in each, and a quotation from the Canadian report represents the social and economic trends in the contributing countries:

“Canadians are marrying at an earlier age than before; they are living longer; they are going to school longer; more women of all ages (particularly married women) are in the labour force; the unquestioned authority of the male is being replaced by a sharing of family authority and responsibility by the husband and wife, and in some cases by the children; incomes have been continually rising; the trend towards urban living coupled with an increase in suburban living is increasing rapidly; transportation facilities by road, rail, air and water are facilitating the mobility of the people; mass communication via the printed word, radio, and television brings a constant barrage of Home Economics information, and in some cases misinformation, into nearly every Canadian home.”

The President of the Congress was Miss Isobel S.

Reports were presented on the Congress theme by Canada, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Israel, Netherlands, New Zealand, Norway, Sweden, United Kingdom and the United States of America. Great similarity appeared in each, and a quotation from the Canadian report represents the social and economic trends in the contributing countries:

“Canadians are marrying at an earlier age than before; they are living longer; they are going to school longer; more women of all ages (particularly married women) are in the labour force; the unquestioned authority of the male is being replaced by a sharing of family authority and responsibility by the husband and wife, and in some cases by the children; incomes have been continually rising; the trend towards urban living coupled with an increase in suburban living is increasing rapidly; transportation facilities by road, rail, air and water are facilitating the mobility of the people; mass communication via the printed word, radio, and television brings a constant barrage of Home Economics information, and in some cases misinformation, into nearly every Canadian home.”

The President of the Congress was Miss Isobel S.

brief_context: Location used for official functions before the Mansion House.
brief_extract: Until the Mansion House was built the Lord Mayor had no official residence; he lived in his own house in the City or rented one for his term of office, using one of the Livery Companies’ Halls for entertaining on a large scale. Guildhall was only used for important official banquets and ceremonies or for dealing with municipal affairs. In 1728 the Court of Common Council set up a Committee to decide upon a site for building an official residence for the Lord Mayor, and having eventually chosen the site of the Stocks Market they opened a limited competition to well-known architects to submit designs.

Visiting the Mansion House today it is interesting to let one’s imagination slip back into the past and conjure up a picture of the gatherings held there in 1753. The gentlemen in knee breeches and cuffed coats, set off by gorgeous brocade waistcoats trimmed with fancy buttons, accompanied by their ladies in handsome silks with charming lace caps on their hair strolling round in the soft mellow glow from hundreds of candles; or the stately Victorians admiring the sparkling gas-lit chandeliers.

article_title: A Trip to South Africa with Mr. and Mrs. Gregory
brief_extract: They boarded a 1932 charabanc and went through the town gateway with its heavy iron doors; and among many introductions there was one to the Governor's 240-year-old tortoise. A three-and-a-half day voyage brought them to Cape Town, a "sort of Charing Cross for world shipping". The main street is flanked by skyscrapers, and in the various emporiums prices were often cheaper than at home.

article_title: A Trip to South Africa with Mr. and Mrs. Gregory
brief_extract: George's Anglican Cathedral; and Cape Town Castle, founded by the Dutch in 1666. The western coast of the Cape Peninsula provided a grand panorama of seaside resorts at the foot of the Table Mountain, and after a cold and windy voyage round the Cape of Good Hope, Port Elizabeth was reached. Here the coloured people were of a different type from those in Cape Town; some were smartly dressed and occasionally a native housewife had her baby on her back and a shopping basket on her head.

brief_context: Location where unique granite rock formations were observed.
brief_extract:
Visits from Salisbury
Visits from Salisbury revealed the grandeur
of the surrounding and distant country, the
peculiar geological formation of rocks, the great
agricultural enterprises which depend on hydro-
electric power, and the incipient townships soon
to become industrial cities. One frequently sees granite blocks, high as a
three-storey house; one, at Epworth, had four
boulders balanced on top of each other with
an inch of touching surface. During one visit
the Gregorys passed a Government native
school for agriculture and various trades, and
noticed the contour cultivation to prevent
erosion.

brief_extract:
The Journey Home
Many thousands of miles must necessarily
be telescoped into a few paragraphs, and much
of the long rail journey was spent at night. A
change of train was made at industrial Bula-
wayo; historic Mafeking was passed while pas-
sengers slept. Kimberley, with its railway
yards like Birmingham, was left behind, and
after the descent from the highlands to a valley
with miles of vine plantation and fruit, the
motive power changed from steam to electricity.

location_standardised: Halifax, West Yorkshire, England, United Kingdom
brief_context: A distant location from which children travel to the school.
brief_extract: This house was taken over by the National Spastics Society and opened by them as a School in 1955, to provide education and therapy for approximately 40 children between the ages of 5 and 16. These children come from all parts of the country, some as far afield as Halifax and Bournemouth and some as near to Cardiff as Monmouth and Carmarthen. In June of last year a new school block was opened, and this filled a long-felt want for modern classrooms, where everything is geared to fit the needs of its handicapped occupants.

brief_extract:
MISS MARY GEORGE, E.A.W. DIRECTOR, discusses an important aspect of
Electricity in Scotland
ONE of the greatest problems of the elec- tricity supply industry is how to give us the constantly increasing supplies of power we need to support our expanding economy and rising standards of living without unduly trespassing on the countryside and detracting from the natural amenities. Power stations take up a large amount of space and this means that nowadays they have to fight for a share of our precious open country.

brief_extract: During a recent tour that our National Presi- dent, Lady Kilmuir, and I made in Scotland, we were particularly interested to see how the two Scottish Electricity Boards were coping with this problem. Hunterston, the nuclear power station which is being constructed for the South of Scotland Electricity Board on the coast of Ayrshire, has been subjected to particularly heavy criticism. The site is a beautiful one on a promontory jutting out into the Firth of Clyde opposite the island of Great Cumbrae with the Arran Peaks in the distance.

The new factory known as Barlaston, was carefully planned and there are now nearly 2,000 employees producing new designs, as well as old favourites, in workshops that give the craftsmen and women every possible scientific and mechanical aid. There is no longer any smoke belching from bottle kilns, so typical of the potteries landscape, for this is an all-electric factory; the kilns are electrically heated tunnels 100 yards long and were the first to be installed in the area, thus ensuring continuous production of Queen's Ware (fine earthenware), bone china, Black Basalt and Jasper in clean surroundings free from smoke and dirt.

brief_context: Subject of electrical generation and consumption statistics.
brief_extract: We did, however, have one great achievement to our credit — the 132kV Grid started before the Depression but finished during those years, linking together our major power stations and thus effecting great economies in the generation of electricity. Since that date, electrical generation in Great Britain has risen by five times, and the price to the domestic consumer has not risen more than two to two and a half times, whereas the cost of living has risen by a greater factor than this. Our homes consume three to four times more electricity than they did twenty-five years ago, our factories in general are very well lit, mechanisation—using electricity—has invaded many industrial processes thus increasing productivity by a large ratio, our streets are better lit and there is a large amount of electrical traction, but the consumption of electricity per head of the population is only one half of the figure of the U.S.A.

location_standardised: Calder Hall, Cumbria, England, United Kingdom
brief_context: Location of the nuclear power station connected to the grid.
brief_extract: In my 1946 Faraday Lecture when I described these developments of nuclear science, I said I thought we might have the first large power station in ten years; I allowed five years for raising the temperature of the wartime nuclear reactor to a high value and five years to produce an engineered version. Fortunately for my reputation Her Majesty the Queen connected Calder Hall to the Grid in October, 1956, and we now stand on the brink of a vast new development: in ten years after Calder we shall be generating half as much electricity from the fission of uranium as we now generate from coal. Of course, in that same ten years our consumption of electricity in Great Britain is likely to rise by a factor of two, so we must get that increase from coal—or oil-fired stations—to the extent that we cannot get it from uranium.

brief_context: Reference for the size of a new nuclear station.
brief_extract:
Already by 1969 it is likely that nuclear stations will deliver electricity at rates as low as modern coal stations now. Over the twenty-five years, we could expect continuing modest improve- ments in the efficiency of coal-fired power stations, but in the new technology of nuclear powered stations you might see dramatic advances; already the latest nuclear station to be placed on order is five times bigger than Calder, and this improvement is due to simple advances of engineering. Railways electrified

We can expect all rail traction to be electric, not diesel electric, that is only a stop-gap mea- sure till all lines are electrified, and as all the electricity will come from nuclear energy we eliminate 12 million tons of coal and a great deal of dirt.
